video_title: Fed Turns Hawkish, Spurs Surge in Rate Hike Bets | The China Show 6/18/2026
gist: Bloomberg's The China Show covers Kevin Warsh's first FOMC as Fed chair, where the Fed held rates, shortened the statement, dropped forward guidance and published a split dot plot that pushed traders to fully price a hike by October. Guests split sharply: Rob Kaplan warns the dots were submitted before the Iran peace deal and may overstate hawkishness, while Nancy Davis argues markets misread Warsh entirely and that higher rate vol and a steeper curve are the real trade. Secondary threads: PBOC overnight repo plumbing, MSCI China on bear-market watch amid record tech dispersion, the G7 rare-earth de-risking target, and WeRide's robotaxi push into Madrid and Zurich.

themes.theme: Warsh communication reset at the Fed

insights.claim: Kevin Warsh used his first FOMC meeting as Fed chair to shorten the policy statement, drop forward guidance entirely, and withhold his own dot from the dot plot, marking a deliberate break in Fed communication practice.
insights.speaker: Yvonne and David, hosts
insights.so_what: Less official guidance means market pricing, not Fed speak, becomes the transmission channel; positioning must be built off data prints rather than speeches.
insights.quote: WE DROPPED FORWARD GUIDANCE. THIS COMMITTEE WILL DELIVER PRICE STABILITY.

insights.claim: Warsh is standing up task forces in five areas central to the conduct of monetary policy, signalling an institutional overhaul of Fed practice rather than a purely rate-focused chairmanship.
insights.speaker: Kevin Warsh
insights.so_what: Framework and balance-sheet review headlines over the next year are a live source of rates and QT-related volatility beyond the policy rate itself.
insights.quote: I'M APPOINTING A TASK FORCE IN EACH OF FIVE AREAS THAT ARE ESSENTIAL TO BROAD CONDUCT OF MONETARY POLICY.

insights.claim: Warsh framed the Fed as having missed its own 2% inflation goal for more than five years, using the miss to justify a hard commitment to delivering price stability.
insights.speaker: Kevin Warsh
insights.so_what: A chair anchoring credibility on a five-year overshoot raises the bar for cuts and lowers the bar for an insurance hike.
insights.quote: WE RECOGNIZE THAT INFLATION HAS BEEN RUNNING WELL AHEAD OF THE FED'S LONG STATED INFLATION GOAL OF 2%. THAT'S BEEN GOING ON FOR MORE THAN FIVE YEARS.

insights.claim: Rob Kaplan says Warsh will be careful even about describing the Fed's reaction function, which leaves the FOMC statement itself as the best available guide for markets.
insights.speaker: Rob Kaplan, Goldman Sachs vice chairman and former Dallas Fed president
insights.so_what: Statement wording changes become higher-information events; the reaction-function vacuum argues for owning rate optionality into meetings.
insights.quote: WE LEARNED THAT HE IS SERIOUS ABOUT NOT WANTING TO MAKE PREDICTIONS OR GIVE FORWARD GUIDANCE.

insights.claim: Kaplan argues the unspoken debate inside the Fed is a three-way tension between an inflationary US AI and infrastructure capex boom straining labour and resources, a disinflationary AI adoption boom still over the horizon, and a war whose end should relieve prices.
insights.speaker: Rob Kaplan
insights.so_what: A usable map for scoring incoming data: capex prints are hawkish inputs, AI-adoption productivity and lower energy are dovish offsets.
insights.quote: IT'S A TENSION BETWEEN AN INFRASTRUCTURE BOOM, CAPEX, AI RELATED, A INFRASTRUCTURE RELATED BOOM IN THE U.S. WHICH IS PROBABLY INFLATIONARY.

insights.claim: Nancy Davis says the key signal from Warsh was not a hike but that the Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI calculation is being discarded and recalculated away from survey data, with some non-BLS inflation measures already running under 2%.
insights.speaker: Nancy Davis, founder and CEO of Quadratic Capital Management
insights.so_what: If the official inflation gauge is reconstructed lower, the hawkish repricing in front-end rates and breakevens is vulnerable to reversal.
insights.quote: IT IS NOT REAL MEASURE OF INFLATION, IT IS OUT THE WINDOW. AND THEY WILL BE RECALCULATING.

insights.claim: Traders moved a Fed rate hike forward from March next year to October and have now almost fully priced a second hike by the first quarter of next year following the hawkish dot plot.
insights.speaker: David, host
insights.so_what: Front-end US rates now embed roughly two hikes; any dovish surprise on inflation is asymmetric for receivers.

insights.claim: The FOMC is split roughly half and half, with nine committee members seeing higher rates or a hike this year and the other half seeing rates hold steady or decline.
insights.speaker: Yvonne, host
insights.so_what: A 50/50 committee under a chair who refuses guidance means meeting-by-meeting outcome risk stays elevated and swap pricing will whipsaw.

insights.claim: Kaplan says that if inflation prints have not cooled by September the Fed will face overwhelming pressure to act, and that this is a reality pressure rather than a market pressure.
insights.speaker: Rob Kaplan
insights.so_what: September is the decision node; summer CPI and PCE prints are the tradable catalysts for the front end.
insights.quote: I DON'T THINK THAT IS A MARKET PRESSURE. I THINK THAT IS A REALITY PRESSURE. THEY'VE GOT SOME TIME, BUT I DON'T KNOW THEY HAVE A LOT OF TIME BEYOND SEPTEMBER.

insights.claim: Kaplan warns the dot plot is stale because participants submitted their projections the Thursday or Friday before the meeting, prior to the Iran war coming to an end, so a dot plot done six weeks later would likely be softer than the nine hawkish dots suggest.
insights.speaker: Rob Kaplan
insights.so_what: The hawkish repricing rests on pre-peace-deal inputs, and there is no new dot plot until September, so the market is trading a data set that is already obsolete.
insights.quote: IF I WERE IN MY FORMER SEAT, I WOULD BE URGING CAUTION ABOUT OVER INTERPRETING THIS DOT PLOT BECAUSE WE JUST HAD A BIG CHANGE, AND I WANT TO GIVE A CHANCE FOR THAT TO WORK THROUGH THE SYSTEM.

insights.claim: Kaplan argues that a September Fed move would not be a one-off insurance hike because historically the Fed rarely acts once, with moves normally coming in twos and threes, implying a second hike before March.
insights.speaker: Rob Kaplan
insights.so_what: Justifies the market pricing a second hike by Q1 and argues against fading the whole hiking path if September delivers.
insights.quote: NORMALLY, THESE MOVES COME IN TWOS AND THREES.

insights.claim: Nancy Davis takes the opposite side, arguing hikes are not the right framing and that on probabilities the Fed is more likely to cut later this year, with Warsh simply unwilling to look dovish at his first meeting while building consensus.
insights.speaker: Nancy Davis
insights.so_what: If she is right, the October hike pricing is the mispricing, and a steepener plus long front-end receivers is the expression.
insights.quote: I DID NOT HEAR THAT A HIKE IS COMING. THAT WAS NOT MY TAKE AWAY, ALTHOUGH THE MARKET DISAGREES.

themes.theme: Curve shape, term premium and the return of rate vol

insights.claim: Kaplan says the long end of the Treasury curve is now driven far more by Treasury supply and demand and deficit expectations than by the Fed, whose disproportionate influence sits at the front end.
insights.speaker: Rob Kaplan
insights.so_what: Trade the front end off Fed policy and the back end off fiscal supply; Fed hawkishness alone is not a reason to be short 10s and 30s.
insights.quote: I THINK THE BACK END OF THE CURVE IS BEING DRIVEN MUCH MORE BY NOT THE FED BUT BY SUPPLY DEMAND OF TREASURIES AND EXPECTATIONS FOR HOW BIG THE DEFICIT IS GOING TO BE.

insights.claim: Kaplan flags that US government net debt to GDP is now over 100% versus the mid-70s pre-COVID, a jump in leverage that is a global rather than purely American condition.
insights.speaker: Rob Kaplan
insights.so_what: Structurally higher term premium is the base case; duration is a poor hedge against growth shocks at these debt levels.

insights.claim: Kaplan argues that with historically high global leverage and very limited workforce growth, all of the growth needed for deleveraging has to come from productivity, which is what the long end is really reacting to.
insights.speaker: Rob Kaplan
insights.so_what: Makes AI-driven productivity the single most important variable for long-end yields and for whether debt loads are sustainable.
insights.quote: THAT MEANS ALL OF OUR GROWTH FOR DELEVERAGING HAS TO COME FROM PRODUCTIVITY.

insights.claim: Nancy Davis says the market produced a massive flattening because everyone focused on hikes and nobody was paying attention to the back end, and she expects steeper curves as a normal term premium returns.
insights.speaker: Nancy Davis
insights.so_what: Positions the flattening as a positioning artifact and steepeners as the higher-conviction expression of the Warsh regime.
insights.quote: WE WILL SEE STEEPER CURVES WITH MORE OF A NORMAL TERM PREMIUM COMING BACK TO THE MARKET.

insights.claim: Davis notes the US 2s10s spread is normally around 100 basis points and is nowhere near that today, even as the Japanese 10-year spread is over 100 basis points, framing the US curve as anomalously flat.
insights.speaker: Nancy Davis
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete target for steepener sizing and a cross-market benchmark in JGBs.

insights.claim: Davis says US interest rate volatility has fallen by over 50% in the last three years since the Silicon Valley Bank peak in 2023, an abnormal environment sustained by forward guidance that Warsh has now removed.
insights.speaker: Nancy Davis
insights.so_what: Removing guidance removes the vol suppressant; long rate vol is the direct trade on the regime change.
insights.quote: INTEREST RATE VOLATILITY HAS FALLEN BY OVER 50% IN THE LAST THREE YEARS IN THE U.S. THAT IS CRAZY.

insights.claim: Davis warns that with credit spreads super tight, investors have been selling optionality to yield-enhance their credit exposure, and those option-selling strategies are in for a rude awakening as volatility rises.
insights.speaker: Nancy Davis
insights.so_what: Identifies short-vol yield-enhancement structures as the crowded pain trade if rate vol normalises higher.
insights.quote: A LOT OF STRATEGIES OUT THERE THAT SELL OPTIONS AND THEY ARE IN FOR A RUDE AWAKENING.

themes.theme: Dollar, yen and Asia FX after the hawkish Fed

insights.claim: ANZ's Mahjabeen Zaman argues peak hawkishness is already in the price for the US dollar and struggles to identify what else could take it higher from here.
insights.speaker: Mahjabeen Zaman, head of FX research at ANZ
insights.so_what: Argues against chasing dollar strength on the hawkish Fed repricing and favours fading the move.
insights.quote: WE THINK PEAK HAWKISHNESS IS ALREADY IN THE PRICE. WHAT ELSE CAN TAKE THE DOLLAR HIGHER? I'M NOT SURE.

insights.claim: Zaman says the US exceptionalism story hinges on positive wealth effects from US risk assets while US consumer and household savings are at their lowest, making the underlying consumer weaker than the narrative implies.
insights.speaker: Mahjabeen Zaman
insights.so_what: Links dollar strength to equity performance; an equity drawdown would remove the wealth-effect prop and accelerate dollar downside.

insights.claim: ANZ retains a weaker-dollar lean into year end on the view that a reopened Strait of Hormuz and lower oil prices will lift the badly sold-off energy-importing currencies, with the euro as the anti-dollar proxy set to outperform.
insights.speaker: Mahjabeen Zaman
insights.so_what: Gives an explicit causal chain from Hormuz reopening to long EUR, GBP and JPY versus the dollar.

insights.claim: Dollar-yen is trading around 160.63 post-Fed, approaching the weakest level in two years, with the market watching for Japanese intervention timed after the Fed decision.
insights.speaker: Yvonne, host
insights.so_what: A concrete intervention watch level; a break of the 2024 low is the trigger for official action and gap risk.

insights.claim: Zaman argues yen intervention will not help much because unilateral intervention in April and May failed, and that a genuinely stronger yen requires a super hawkish Bank of Japan which markets did not get this time.
insights.speaker: Mahjabeen Zaman
insights.so_what: Fading intervention-driven yen rallies remains viable until the BOJ turns genuinely hawkish or intervention becomes coordinated.
insights.quote: TO GET A STRONGER YEN, WE NEED A SUPER HAWKISH BANK OF JAPAN. WE DIDN'T GET THAT THIS TIME, SLOW NORMALIZATION IS THE MESSAGE.

insights.claim: ANZ expects one more Bank of Japan rate hike in the fourth quarter and sees the yen strengthening into next year as inflation returns and real wages turn positive, subject to resolving Japan's fiscal volatility.
insights.speaker: Mahjabeen Zaman
insights.so_what: A dated catalyst for JPY longs and for JGB positioning going into Q4.
insights.quote: WE THINK THERE WILL BE ONE MORE RATE HIKE BY THE BANK OF JAPAN IN Q4

insights.claim: Zaman favours the Australian dollar as the way to fade dollar strength in G10, citing carry after three RBA hikes with the RBA now on hold, cyclical leverage to a global growth recovery if the war ends, and Australia's net energy exporter status.
insights.speaker: Mahjabeen Zaman
insights.so_what: A specific G10 long expressing both the carry and the peace-deal growth trade, though the energy-exporter edge may partially claw back.

themes.theme: PBOC plumbing, not a policy-rate pivot

insights.claim: Bloomberg Economics' David Chiu says the PBOC's overnight reverse repo changes are liquidity management rather than a framework shift, because the PBOC only overhauled its rate framework two years ago when it made the seven-day reverse repo the key policy rate.
insights.speaker: David Chiu, Bloomberg Economics
insights.so_what: Warns against trading Chinese rates as if a Fed-style overnight policy rate has arrived; the seven-day rate remains the anchor to watch.
insights.quote: WE DON'T THINK THAT IS A SIGNAL FOR THE CHANGE OF THE FRAMEWORK, BECAUSE THE PBOC JUST OVERHAULED IT TWO YEARS AGO.

insights.claim: The PBOC narrowed the 50 basis point spread it had allowed the overnight market rate to deviate from the seven-day policy rate and moved the overnight operation window one hour earlier to give banks more time to manage liquidity.
insights.speaker: David Chiu
insights.so_what: Mechanically compresses month-end and quarter-end funding spikes in China, lowering a recurring source of onshore rate volatility.

insights.claim: Chiu links the PBOC's move to leverage concerns as the 10-year Chinese government bond yield has dropped about 12 basis points year to date with traders rushing into bonds, invoking the June 2013 squeeze when the overnight rate spiked to around 30%.
insights.speaker: David Chiu
insights.so_what: Signals the PBOC is pre-positioning against a bond-market leverage unwind; onshore duration longs face policy-driven squeeze risk into quarter end.

insights.claim: A Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance professor expects the PBOC to keep pushing the overnight repo rate as the guidance rate over the LPR, with more clarity by the end of the year, and sees the next cut probably this year but highly dependent on the international and inflation environment.
insights.speaker: finance professor, Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance
insights.so_what: Sets a year-end checkpoint for whether China's policy anchor migrates, which would change how onshore rates and the yuan trade.

insights.claim: The professor argues slowing Chinese credit growth is by design as China shifts from a debt and credit driven growth model to a technology and innovation driven one, meaning growth will come from new energy vehicles, AI and high-end semiconductors rather than credit-intensive housing.
insights.speaker: finance professor, Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance
insights.so_what: Reframes weak Chinese credit data as intentional rather than a stimulus failure, arguing against buying property-linked cyclicals on credit weakness.
insights.quote: I THINK CHINA IS TRYING TO ENGINEER ITS GROWTH FOR MORE DEBT DRIVEN OR CREDIT DRIVEN TO THE MORE TECHNOLOGY OR INNOVATION DRIVEN MODEL.

themes.theme: China equities: bear-market watch amid record tech dispersion

insights.claim: MSCI China is about 19% below its October peak and roughly one point from the 20% drawdown that would mark a technical bear market, with the index trading around the 7,382 level and the threshold in the low 7,200s.
insights.speaker: David, host
insights.so_what: A hard, published trigger level; a formal bear-market print is a mechanical catalyst for systematic and headline-driven flows.

insights.claim: The Hang Seng is set for a fifth consecutive weekly loss, which would be the longest such streak in about 11 years, with Friday closed so the session is the last of the week.
insights.speaker: David, host
insights.so_what: Multi-year streak extremes are the kind of statistic that attracts mean-reversion capital and marks sentiment washouts.

insights.claim: Anthony Stevens argues equity markets are splitting into equities and techquities, with the semiconductor and AI supply chain including optical components outperforming while hyperscalers and Chinese platforms drag MSCI China down.
insights.speaker: Anthony Stevens, guest
insights.so_what: Argues for expressing Asia tech through semis and optical suppliers rather than index or platform exposure.
insights.quote: EQUITY MARKETS ARE SPLITTING INTO EQUITIES AND TECHQUITIES.

insights.claim: Stevens cites Bloomberg Intelligence showing dispersion in Asian equities at a record high, following US dispersion, and holding up despite macro pressure from the Iran war and the Fed, leading him to conclude macro does not matter for these names.
insights.speaker: Anthony Stevens
insights.so_what: Record dispersion favours single-name and pair trades over index beta and supports long-short over directional Asia exposure.
insights.quote: DISPERSION IN ASIAN EQUITIES IS AT A RECORD HIGH

insights.claim: Chinese regulators are drafting rules to curb food delivery subsidies, weighing on Alibaba while Meituan traded up around 2% on the news.
insights.speaker: Yvonne, host
insights.so_what: Subsidy caps end a cash-burn war and are margin-positive for the incumbent platform, which is why the tape rewarded Meituan and punished Alibaba.

insights.claim: Deutsche Bank estimates BYD's flagship SUV presale momentum could add more than 10,000 units of monthly sales.
insights.speaker: Yvonne, host
insights.so_what: A quantified volume delta for the largest Chinese EV maker in a market otherwise dominated by price-war concerns.

insights.claim: The MiniMax long-short pair trade is expected to gain momentum into early July because a large chunk of MiniMax stock is released after the IPO lockup, implying more selling pressure on that leg.
insights.speaker: Yvonne, host
insights.so_what: A dated, mechanical supply catalyst for a crowded AI-adjacent pair trade in Hong Kong.

themes.theme: Iran deal, rare-earth de-risking and defence

insights.claim: Trump signed an interim peace deal with Iran at his visit to France that opens a 60-day negotiating window and includes reopening the Strait of Hormuz, but it is explicitly not a final agreement.
insights.speaker: Jill Disis, Bloomberg
insights.so_what: Oil and energy-importing FX are trading a deal that could still unwind inside 60 days; the risk premium removal is provisional.
insights.quote: IT OPENS THE DOOR FOR 60 DAYS OF NEGOTIATIONS

insights.claim: Trump appeared to walk back longstanding Republican red lines, seeming open to Iranian uranium enrichment, retention of some ballistic missiles, and Iranian access to roughly $100 billion of frozen assets, dismaying Iran hawks in his own party.
insights.speaker: Jill Disis
insights.so_what: Domestic political pushback is the main channel through which the deal could reverse, making Republican rhetoric a leading indicator for oil risk premium.

insights.claim: G7 leaders agreed that by 2030 no single country will supply any member nation with more than 60% of its rare earth needs, potentially falling to 50% after 2030, covering rare earths and permanent magnets with possible extension to other critical minerals this year.
insights.speaker: Stephen Engle, Bloomberg
insights.so_what: A dated, quantified de-risking target that underwrites the investment case for non-Chinese rare earth miners, processors and recyclers.
insights.quote: NO SINGLE COUNTRY WILL BE ABLE TO, BY 2030, PROVIDE EACH NATION WITH MORE THAN 60% OF THEIR RARE EARTH NEEDS.

insights.claim: Engle is sceptical the G7 target is achievable given China controls upwards of 90% of some rare earths and Japan still procures about 75% of its rare earths from China even after 16 years of living with Chinese export controls dating to 2010.
insights.speaker: Stephen Engle
insights.so_what: Japan is the natural experiment showing diversification takes more than a decade, so China retains supply leverage well past 2030.
insights.quote: THEY STILL PROCURE ABOUT 75%, STILL AFTER 16 YEARS OF THE EXPORT CONTROLS, STILL ABOUT 75% OF RARE-EARTH FROM CHINA.

insights.claim: Japan's defence minister says the long-standing 1% of GDP spending cap prevented allocating funding where it was genuinely needed, and questions the transparency and evidential basis of China's official military spending figures.
insights.speaker: Japan's defense minister
insights.so_what: Signals Japanese defence budgets will be set by capability requirements rather than a GDP percentage, a structural tailwind for Japanese defence and drone suppliers.

insights.claim: WeRide, with Uber and partners, will launch commercial robotaxi services in Madrid and Zurich later this year, its fourth and fifth joint deployment cities, working with Madrid's regional government and Switzerland's federal road office.
insights.speaker: Tony Han, founder and CEO of WeRide
insights.so_what: First commercial robotaxi footholds in continental Europe establish the regulatory template competitors will have to match.

insights.claim: WeRide plans to roll out 15 cities before 2030 and Tony Han expects the majority of the next ten cities after Madrid and Zurich to be in Europe, subject to regulatory approval and negotiations with local operators.
insights.speaker: Tony Han
insights.so_what: Concentrates WeRide's expansion risk in European regulatory approvals rather than US or Chinese licensing.

insights.claim: WeRide runs an asset-light strategy partnering with local taxi operators and Uber, and has deployed autonomous driving products in 40 cities across 12 countries with approximately 3,000 autonomous vehicles of which 1,300 are robotaxis and 500 are overseas.
insights.speaker: Tony Han
insights.so_what: Concrete fleet base to benchmark against Waymo and Baidu, and the asset-light model changes the capital intensity of scaling.
insights.quote: CURRENTLY WE HAVE APPROXIMATELY 3000 AUTONOMOUS DRIVING VEHICLES. 1300 VEHICLES ARE ROBOTAXIS.

insights.claim: China suspended issuing new autonomous vehicle licences after the outage that hit Baidu's robotaxi fleet in Wuhan, but Tony Han says WeRide's licence pipeline is intact and expects the suspension not to last long, having lobbied that one company's mistake should not halt the whole industry.
insights.speaker: Tony Han
insights.so_what: A CEO-sourced view that the Chinese AV licensing freeze is temporary, which is the key regulatory overhang on the sector's domestic growth.
insights.quote: OVERALL I AM RELATIVELY OPTIMISTIC, AND I'M NOT CONCERNED ABOUT A HALT. THIS KIND OF SUSPENSION WILL NOT LAST LONG.

insights.claim: The market expects WeRide to roughly double revenue this year from $1 billion to just over $2.1 billion for full year 2026, and Tony Han says he thinks the company will achieve that target despite the stock price not yet reflecting progress.
insights.speaker: Tony Han and David, host
insights.so_what: A CEO effectively endorsing consensus revenue doubling is the single most tradable disclosure in the interview.
